claim: Penicillin and related antibiotics disrupt cell wall synthesis to induce bacteriolysis.
source: Penicillin and related antibiotics disrupt cell wall synthesis to induce bacteriolysis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the manuscript (Park, 1964; Park and Strominger, 1957).

claim: Lysis in response to penicillin requires the activity of cell wall hydrolases called autolysins.
source: Lysis in response to these drugs requires the activity of cell wall hydrolases called autolysins, but how penicillins misactivate these deadly enzymes has long remained unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and is a known fact in the field.

claim: During exponential growth, Streptococcus pneumoniae cells primarily produce lipid-anchored teichoic acids (LTAs) that bind and sequester the major autolysin LytA.
source: We find that during exponential growth, Sp cells primarily produce lipid-anchored TAs called lipoteichoic acids (LTAs) that bind and sequester the major autolysin LytA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4, 5, and related analyses showing LTA levels and LytA localization during exponential growth.

claim: Penicillin-treatment or prolonged stationary phase growth triggers the degradation of a key LTA synthase in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: However, penicillin-treatment or prolonged stationary phase growth triggers the degradation of a key LTA synthase, causing a switch to the production of wall-anchored TAs (WTAs).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing TacL degradation under these conditions.

claim: The switch from LTA to WTA production allows LytA to associate with and degrade its cell wall substrate, promoting osmotic lysis.
source: This change allows LytA to associate with and degrade its cell wall substrate, thus promoting osmotic lysis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5 and 6 showing LytA relocalization to the cell wall and increased WTA levels at the onset of lysis.

claim: Beta-lactams covalently modify the transpeptidase active site of penicillin-binding proteins to block peptidoglycan crosslinking activity.
source: Beta-lactams covalently modify the TP active site of the PBPs to block the PG crosslinking activity of the aPBPs and SEDS-bPBP complexes (Cho et al., 2016; Tipper and Strominger, 1965).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Beta-lactam-induced lysis in Streptococcus pneumoniae is dependent on the activity of the peptidoglycan cleaving enzyme LytA.
source: However, pioneering studies from Tomasz and co-workers in the Gram-positive pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae (Sp) changed this view by showing that lysis in this organism was dependent on the activity of a PG cleaving enzyme called LytA (Tomasz et al., 1970; Tomasz and Waks, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 1A.

claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae requires a single peptidoglycan hydrolase called LytA for lysis-induction.
source: It has the advantage of requiring a single PG hydrolase called LytA for lysis-induction (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Tomasz et al., 1970; Tomasz and Waks, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating that ΔlytA mutants do not lyse in response to penicillin.

claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae cells lyse following prolonged growth in stationary phase.
source: Another benefit of Sp is its propensity to lyse following prolonged growth in stationary phase (Fernebro et al., 2004; Mellroth et al., 2012; Tomasz et al., 1970; Tomasz and Waks, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by growth curve data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Autolysis in stationary phase is LytA-dependent in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: Like penicillin-induced lysis, autolysis in stationary phase is LytA-dependent (Fernebro et al., 2004; Mellroth et al., 2012; Tomasz et al., 1970; Tomasz and Waks, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing ΔlytA mutants do not lyse in stationary phase.

claim: LytA protein levels remain constant during growth in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: Previous studies indicated that LytA protein levels remain constant during growth, and we have confirmed this result (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Fernebro et al., 2004; Henriques Normark and Normark, 2002; Mellroth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LytA activity is negatively regulated during normal exponential growth by an inhibitory factor(s).
source: Based on this observation, we hypothesized that LytA activity is negatively regulated during normal exponential growth by an inhibitory factor(s).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the observation that LytA levels remain constant but activity changes.

claim: The gene tacL is virtually devoid of transposon insertions in wild-type Streptococcus pneumoniae but readily inactivated in ΔlytA mutants.
source: When the insertion profiles were compared, we found that the gene tacL (SPD_1672) was virtually devoid of insertions in the WT library, but readily inactivated by insertions in the ΔlytA library (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Tn-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TacL depletion causes premature LytA-dependent autolysis in exponential phase.
source: Furthermore, TacL depletion during growth in liquid medium caused premature LytA-dependent autolysis in exponential phase (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data in Figure 2C.

claim: TacL is required for the growth-phase-dependent control of LytA activity at a step after its export to the cell surface.
source: We therefore conclude that TacL is required for the growth-phase-dependent control of LytA activity at a step after its export to the cell surface.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data in Figure 3B showing that ΔtacL cells are sensitive to exogenously added LytA during exponential growth.

claim: TacL is a polytopic membrane protein predicted to have a large extracellular loop domain.
source: TacL is a polytopic membrane protein predicted to have a large extracellular loop domain (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction and is illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: WTA and LTA in Streptococcus pneumoniae cells have identical main chains.
source: Unlike most firmicutes, WTA and LTA in Sp cells have identical main chains (Brown et al., 2013; Denapaite et al., 2012; Fischer et al., 1993; Gisch et al., 2013; Heß et al., 2017; Percy and Gründling, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae cells make WTAs and LTAs from a common precursor polymer linked to an undecaprenyl phosphate lipid carrier.
source: Furthermore, bioinformatic analysis indicates that Sp cells are likely to make WTAs and LTAs from a common precursor polymer linked to an undecaprenyl phosphate (Und-P) lipid carrier (Figure 4A) (Denapaite et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and prior work, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: TacL is likely to be the LTA synthase in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: A recent study using mass spectrometry found that TacL is likely to be the corresponding LTA synthase (Heß et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent mass spectrometry study.

claim: TacL transfers the TA polymer from undecaprenyl phosphate to the glycolipid anchor diglucosyl-diacylglycerol to form LTAs.
source: It is thought to be responsible for transferring the TA polymer from Und-P to the glycolipid anchor diglucosyl-diacylglycerol (Glc2-DAG) to form LTAs (Figure 4A) and was therefore renamed TacL for teichoic acid ligase (Heß et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: TacL shares remote similarity with O-antigen ligases.
source: Consistent with this assignment, HHPred analysis indicates that TacL shares remote similarity with O-antigen ligases (99.7% probability, E-value 5.1e-13) (Heß et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2014), enzymes from Gram-negative bacteria that carry out a similar reaction, the transfer of O-antigen glycan polymers from Und-P to a lipid A-core glycolipid acceptor (Kalynych et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis (HHPred) and citations to prior work.

claim: TacL is required for LTA formation in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: As expected based on the recent mass spectrometry study, the signal for this material was dramatically reduced in the ∆tacL strain and was restored upon complementation with tacL expressed from an ectopic locus (Figure 4B) (Heß et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B showing reduced LTA levels in ΔtacL mutants.

claim: TacL-defective cells have a striking increase in WTAs compared to wild-type cells.
source: However, TacL-defective cells had a striking increase in WTAs that was reduced back to near wild-type levels upon tacL complementation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4B showing increased WTA levels in ΔtacL mutants.

claim: The LTA and WTA synthesis pathways are antagonistic and likely compete for the shared undecaprenyl phosphate-linked precursor.
source: Furthermore, the finding that WTAs increase when LTA synthesis is blocked suggests that the two pathways are antagonistic and are likely competing for the shared Und-P linked precursor (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WTA levels increase when LTA synthesis is blocked.

claim: LytA possesses an array of six choline-binding domains that promote its association with phosphocholine-modified teichoic acids.
source: Connecting these two phenomena is that LytA not only has a cell wall cleaving amidase domain, but also possesses an array of six choline-binding domains (CBDs) that promote its association with PCho-modified teichoic acids (Fernández-Tornero et al., 2001; Li et al., 2015; Sandalova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: In TacL+ cells during exponential phase, robust LTA production is observed and low levels of WTAs are detected.
source: In TacL+ cells, we observed robust LTA production in exponential phase (E) and low levels of WTAs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: A significant portion of LytA in TacL+ cells during exponential phase is found in the membrane fraction, presumably through association with LTAs.
source: A significant portion of LytA(H26A) in these samples was found in the membrane fraction, presumably through association with LTAs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5A and 5B showing LytA localization.

claim: As cells reach late stationary phase when autolysis begins, LTA levels are dramatically reduced while WTA levels increase.
source: Finally, as cells reached late stationary phase when autolysis normally begins, LTA levels were dramatically reduced while the amount of WTA had increased relative to the early stationary phase time point (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: At the onset of autolysis, LytA localization switches from the membrane fraction to the cell wall fraction where it is presumably bound to WTAs.
source: Now, LytA(H26A) was no longer found associated with the membrane fraction but instead its localization switched almost entirely to the cell wall fraction where it was presumably bound to the WTAs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5A and 5B showing LytA relocalization.

claim: In ΔtacL cells, WTAs are the only detectable teichoic acids at all growth stages.
source: In similar experiments performed in ΔtacL cells, the WTAs were the only detectable teichoic acids at all growth stages, and LytA(H26A) was found associated with the cell wall fraction at every time point (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: During penicillin-induced autolysis, there is a transition from LTA synthesis to primarily WTA production.
source: We again saw a transition from LTA synthesis before treatment to the production of primarily WTAs at the onset of lysis (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: During penicillin-induced autolysis, extracellular LytA switches from the membrane to cell wall fraction.
source: Extracellular LytA(H26A) similarly was found to switch from the membrane to cell wall fraction during this time course (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Both penicillin-induced and growth-phase-dependent autolysis follow a similar pathway involving a change from LTA to WTA synthesis and an accompanying transition in LytA localization.
source: We therefore conclude that both penicillin-induced and growth-phase-dependent autolysis follow a similar pathway involving a change from LTA to WTA synthesis and an accompanying transition in LytA localization.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data from Figures 5 and 6 showing similar patterns in both conditions.

claim: Streptococcus pneumoniae cells control LytA activity during exponential growth by preferentially producing LTAs over WTAs to keep LytA at the membrane and prevent it from accessing its cell wall substrate.
source: Based on these results, we infer that Sp cells control LytA activity during exponential growth by preferentially producing LTAs over WTAs to keep LytA at the membrane and prevent it from accessing its cell wall substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing LTA production and LytA localization during exponential growth.

claim: In response to prolonged stationary phase growth or treatment with penicillin, the synthetic bias switches such that WTA production becomes favored, resulting in a change in LytA localization to the cell wall where it catalyzes the destruction of the matrix and promotes autolysis.
source: In response to prolonged stationary phase growth or treatment with penicillin, the synthetic bias switches. WTA production becomes favored, resulting in a change in LytA localization to the cell wall where it catalyzes the destruction of the matrix and promotes autolysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing the switch in TA production and LytA localization under autolytic conditions.

claim: Choline-containing TA polymers are released into the medium following treatment of Streptococcus pneumoniae cells with cell wall synthesis inhibitors.
source: Accordingly, Waks and Tomasz, 1978 previously observed the release of choline-containing TA polymers into the medium following treatment of Sp cells with cell wall synthesis inhibitors (Waks and Tomasz, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: As autolysis progresses, an increase in choline-containing material in the supernatant is observed, while LTAs in the membrane become barely detectable at late time points.
source: However, as autolysis progressed, an increase in choline-containing material in the supernatant was observed, while at late time points, LTAs in the membrane were barely detectable (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: LTAs are released from cells during autolysis by an as yet unknown mechanism.
source: Thus, in conjunction with the prior results of Waks and Tomasz, 1978, our results suggest that LTAs are released from cells during autolysis by an as yet unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of choline-containing material in the supernatant and the loss of LTAs from the membrane.

claim: tacL overexpression prevents the induction of autolysis in both stationary-phase growth and penicillin treatment.
source: For both stationary-phase growth and penicillin treatment, tacL overexpression was found to prevent the induction of autolysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), suggesting that a reduction in TacL levels underlies the autolytic switch from LTA to WTA production.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: A reproducible decrease in TacL-FLAG abundance is observed at time points corresponding to autolysis onset.
source: A reproducible decrease in TacL-FLAG abundance was observed at time points corresponding to autolysis onset in a reference LytA+ strain (Figure 8A and B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 8A, 8B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: TacL-FLAG is relatively stable in exponential phase, but its half-life decreases significantly in late stationary phase or in response to penicillin treatment.
source: The protein appeared to be relatively stable in exponential phase, but its half-life decreased significantly in late stationary phase or in response to penicillin treatment (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2C showing TacL stability after chloramphenicol treatment.

claim: TacL degradation is induced in response to conditions that trigger autolysis.
source: We therefore conclude that TacL degradation is induced in response to conditions that trigger autolysis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data showing TacL degradation in stationary phase and after penicillin treatment.

claim: Transposon insertions in ftsH are significantly enriched in the presence of penicillin G compared to no drug or chloramphenicol-treated control.
source: Transposon insertions in ftsH were significantly enriched (p<0.0001) in the presence of PenG compared to no drug or the Cm-treated control.
evidence: This is supported by Tn-Seq data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: FtsH is a highly conserved ATP-dependent zinc metallopeptidase.
source: One of these genes was ftsH, encoding a highly conserved ATP-dependent zinc metallopeptidase (Ito and Akiyama, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: FtsH has two transmembrane segments and a well-known role in the degradation of membrane protein substrates.
source: FtsH has two transmembrane segments and a well-known role in the degradation of membrane protein substrates (Langklotz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: TacL-FLAG remains stable in ΔftsH cells following penicillin treatment.
source: Unlike cells with functional FtsH, TacL-FLAG remained stable in ΔftsH cells following penicillin treatment (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: ΔftsH cells do not undergo the switch in teichoic acid production from LTAs to WTAs following penicillin treatment.
source: Moreover, these cells did not undergo the switch in teichoic acid production from LTAs to WTAs, nor did LytA+ cells lacking FtsH autolyze in response to penicillin treatment (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: LytA+ cells lacking FtsH do not autolyze in response to penicillin treatment.
source: Moreover, these cells did not undergo the switch in teichoic acid production from LTAs to WTAs, nor did LytA+ cells lacking FtsH autolyze in response to penicillin treatment (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 8A and 8B showing growth curves of ΔftsH strains.

claim: TacL-FLAG remains stable in cells lacking FtsH during prolonged stationary phase growth.
source: Specifically, TacL-FLAG remained stable in cells lacking FtsH and LTAs continued to be produced in stationary phase where their levels were dramatically reduced in FtsH+ cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Autolysis in response to cell wall targeting drugs or stationary phase growth is caused by a switch in surface polymer biogenesis triggered by FtsH-mediated degradation of TacL.
source: Altogether, our results support a model in which autolysis in response to cell wall targeting drugs or stationary phase growth is caused by a switch in surface polymer biogenesis triggered by FtsH-mediated degradation of TacL.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing TacL degradation by FtsH and the resulting switch in TA production.

claim: Autolysis of Streptococcus pneumoniae cells following entry into stationary phase was described by Walther Goebl and Oswald Avery almost a century ago.
source: Autolysis of Sp cells following entry into stationary phase was described by Walther Goebl and Oswald Avery almost a century ago (Avery and Cullen, 1923; Goebel and Avery, 1929; Neufeld, 1900).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical work.

claim: Stationary phase autolysis is medically significant due to its relationship with antibiotic-induced bacteriolysis.
source: Although the biological relevance of this phenomenon remains unclear (Eldholm et al., 2009; Hirst et al., 2008; Kietzman et al., 2016; Martner et al., 2009), it is medically significant due to its relationship with antibiotic-induced bacteriolysis (Fernebro et al., 2004; Mellroth et al., 2012; Tomasz et al., 1970; Tomasz and Waks, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The polymeric structure of LTA and WTA is identical in Streptococcus pneumoniae cells.
source: The polymeric structure of LTA and WTA is identical in Sp cells (Denapaite et al., 2012; Fischer et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The differential control exerted by LTAs and WTAs on LytA activity is the result of how they affect the localization of LytA within the cell envelope.
source: Although it is possible that the association of LytA with WTA is required to properly orient the amidase domain with respect to its substrate for productive cleavage (Li et al., 2015; Mellroth et al., 2014; Pérez-Dorado et al., 2010; Sandalova et al., 2016), we favor a model in which the differential control exerted by these polymers is the result of how they affect the localization of LytA within the cell envelope (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Cryoelectron microscopy studies reveal that the peptidoglycan layer in Gram-positive bacteria is spatially separated from the cytoplasmic membrane, forming a 'periplasm'.
source: Cryoelectron microscopy studies of Gram-positive bacteria by Beveridge and co-workers revealed that the PG layer is spatially separated from the cytoplasmic membrane, forming what has been referred to as the Gram-positive 'periplasm' (Matias and Beveridge, 2008; Matias and Beveridge, 2005; Matias and Beveridge, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior cryoelectron microscopy studies.

claim: LTAs are likely to be restricted to the 'periplasmic' space in Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Evidence has also been presented that LTAs are likely to be restricted to this 'periplasmic' space (Matias and Beveridge, 2008; Reichmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The protective function of LTAs is mediated by their ability to bind and sequester LytA in the membrane-proximal zone of the envelope thereby limiting its access to the cell wall.
source: We therefore propose that in Sp cells, the protective function of LTAs is mediated by their ability to bind and sequester LytA in the membrane-proximal zone of the envelope thereby limiting its access to the cell wall and ability to cut bonds in the PG network (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Purified LTAs are capable of inhibiting LytA-mediated autolysis.
source: It is noteworthy that Tomasz and co-workers previously observed that purified LTAs were capable of inhibiting LytA-mediated autolysis by a mechanism that was unclear at the time (Briese and Hakenbeck, 1985; Höltje and Tomasz, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Micellar forms of LTAs can bind and sequester LytA to prevent its association with cell wall substrate.
source: Based on our findings, we infer that these results reflect the ability of micellar forms of LTAs to similarly bind and sequester LytA to prevent its association with cell wall substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and prior observations.

claim: The association of LytA with WTAs is required for cell wall cleavage activity.
source: At this time, LytA is similarly shifted from the membrane to cell wall fractions where it is likely bound to WTAs, its association with which has long been known to be required for cell wall cleavage activity (Giudicelli and Tomasz, 1984; Höltje and Tomasz, 1975; Li et al., 2015; Mellroth et al., 2014; Tipper and Strominger, 1965; Tomasz et al., 1970; Waks and Tomasz, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The change in TA polymer synthesis and subsequent recruitment of LytA from membrane-anchored LTAs to its cell wall substrate underlies autolysis induction.
source: Therefore, our results support a model in which it is the change in TA polymer synthesis and subsequent recruitment of LytA from membrane-anchored LTAs to its cell wall substrate that underlies autolysis induction (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a model supported by the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The switch to WTA synthesis under autolytic conditions involves the degradation of TacL, the likely ligase involved in making LTAs.
source: Although we do not currently know the mechanism by which Sp cells preferentially make LTAs during exponential growth, our results establish that the switch to WTA synthesis under autolytic conditions involves the degradation of TacL, the likely ligase involved in making LTAs (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2) (Heß et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inactivation of the membrane-bound protease FtsH prevents TacL degradation and protects cells from LytA-dependent autolysis.
source: Furthermore, inactivation of the membrane-bound protease FtsH was shown to prevent TacL degradation and protect cells from LytA-dependent autolysis, suggesting that TacL is a direct substrate of FtsH (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: TacL is a direct substrate of FtsH.
source: Furthermore, inactivation of the membrane-bound protease FtsH was shown to prevent TacL degradation and protect cells from LytA-dependent autolysis, suggesting that TacL is a direct substrate of FtsH (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FtsH inactivation prevents TacL degradation.

claim: In Escherichia coli, FtsH controls an important branch point in an envelope biogenesis pathway by targeting LpxC, the enzyme catalyzing the committed step in lipopolysaccharide synthesis.
source: As in Sp cells, E. coli FtsH controls an important branch point in an envelope biogenesis pathway (Ogura et al., 1999). In this case, its key substrate is LpxC, the enzyme catalyzing the committed step in the synthesis of lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a major component of the Gram-negative outer membrane (Führer et al., 2006; Ogura et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on E. coli FtsH.

claim: The LPS and phospholipid synthesis pathways in Escherichia coli compete for fatty acids in the form of acyl-ACP precursors.
source: The LPS and phospholipid synthesis pathways compete for fatty acids in the form of acyl-ACP precursors (Mohan et al., 1994; Normark et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The turnover of LpxC by Escherichia coli FtsH may be regulated by the availability of certain acyl-ACP precursors or the accumulation of downstream products in the LPS synthesis pathway.
source: Indirect evidence suggests that the turnover of LpxC by E. coli FtsH may be regulated by the availability of certain acyl-ACP precursors or the accumulation of downstream products in the LPS synthesis pathway (May and Silhavy, 2018; Mohan et al., 1994; Normark et al., 1969; Ogura et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In Streptococcus pneumoniae, FtsH may respond to precursors or products of the TA polymer assembly pathways it governs.
source: Thus, in Sp cells, FtsH may similarly respond to precursors or products of the TA polymer assembly pathways it governs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on analogy to E. coli FtsH regulation.

claim: The FtsH sensing mechanism might normally function in the homeostatic control of LTA and WTA levels, which may be needed for more precise activation of LytA to promote septal PG cleavage and cell separation.
source: As in E. coli, the sensing mechanism might normally function in the homeostatic control of LTA and WTA levels, which may be needed for more precise activation of LytA to promote septal PG cleavage and cell separation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the normal physiological role of FtsH.

claim: Autolytic conditions would short-circuit the normal balancing mechanism, swinging it too far in favor of WTA synthesis such that destructive levels of LytA activity are stimulated.
source: Autolytic conditions would then be expected to somehow short-circuit the normal balancing mechanism, swinging it too far in favor of WTA synthesis such that destructive levels of LytA activity are stimulated.
evidence: This is a speculation about how autolytic conditions might affect the FtsH regulatory mechanism.

claim: Teichoic acids have been implicated in the control of peptidoglycan hydrolases in other Gram-positive bacteria.
source: TAs have been implicated in the control of PG hydrolases in other Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by the examples provided in the following sentences with citations.

claim: In Staphylococcus aureus, the major autolysin Atl specifically localizes to the septal PG and this localization requires WTA.
source: In Staphylococcus aureus, the major autolysin Atl that acts at division septa to promote cell separation specifically localizes to the septal PG and this localization requires WTA (Schlag et al., 2010; Yamada et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Localization studies suggest that WTA levels are lowest at the septum in Staphylococcus aureus, suggesting that Atl preferentially localizes to PG lacking attached TA polymers.
source: Interestingly, localization studies suggest that WTA levels are lowest at the septum in S. aureus suggesting that Atl preferentially localizes to PG lacking attached TA polymers (Schlag et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, the cell separase LytF localizes to septal PG in a manner that depends on both WTA and LTA.
source: In B. subtilis, the cell separase LytF localizes to septal PG in a manner that depends on both WTA and LTA (Kiriyama et al., 2014; Yamamoto et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The major autolysin AcmA in Lactococcus lactis specifically localizes to the septum while galactosyl-containing TA polymers are largely absent at this site.
source: Finally, the major autolysin AcmA in Lactococcus lactis specifically localizes to the septum while galactosyl-containing TA polymers are largely absent at this site (Steen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In all of these cases the presence of TA polymers appears to interfere with autolysin binding to the cell wall.
source: In all of these cases the presence of TA polymers appears to interfere with autolysin binding to the cell wall, however the mechanisms underlying the temporal and spatial organization/localization of TAs is not known.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited examples.

claim: The interplay between the LTA and WTA synthesis pathways may play a key role in controlling PG hydrolysis and autolytic-induction in other Gram-positive organisms.
source: Although it remains to be investigated, our results in Sp cells suggest that rather than one polymer or the other predominating, it may be the interplay between the LTA and WTA synthesis pathways that plays the key role in controlling PG hydrolysis and autolytic-induction in these and other Gram-positive organisms.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in Sp and the examples from other organisms.
